headline: Washington Canyon fires early as 68-degree water stacks bait on the walls
subhead: Yellowfin and bluefin both showing in the upper water column as June heat kicks the season into gear.
body_markdown:
The Washington is coming alive exactly when it should — three weeks ahead of the other canyons, just like clockwork. That 68-degree water showing up on the buoys tells the whole story. We've got legitimate temperature separation now, and the fish are responding.

Yellowfin are the story this week. Schools of 40 to 60-pounders have been working the northeast wall in 80 to 120 fathoms, and they're not being shy about it. The key has been finding the temperature break where that warm Gulf Stream water meets the cooler shelf water. When you see that 4-degree jump on the fish finder — from 64 to 68 — that's where you want to be.

The bite's been best on the troll, running a spread of cedar plugs and small feathers at 7 to 8 knots. Blue and white cedar plugs on the long riggers, pink and white feathers on the short ones. The fish have been coming up from 60 feet, so keep those baits in the top 40 feet of water. When you mark them, don't be afraid to circle back — these schools are holding tight to structure.

Bluefin are mixed in with the yellowfin, mostly smaller fish in the 40 to 70-inch range, but there's been some bigger fish showing. The northeast corner of the canyon, where it bends toward the 100-fathom line, has been holding the better grade of fish. Same trolling spread works, but when you see the bluefin, switch to chunk bait. Fresh butterfish chunks on 8/0 circles, fished on 50-pound fluorocarbon leaders about 30 feet down.

The mahi bite has been sporadic but worth watching. Small schools of schoolies — 5 to 15 pounds — have been under the scattered weed lines on the southeast wall. They're hitting small ballyhoo on the troll and 3-inch Hogy soft baits when you stop to chunk. The water's still a touch cool for a consistent mahi bite, but it's building.

What's really got my attention is the bait situation. There's been good marks of squid along the 50-fathom line, and that's what's drawing everything in. The yellowfin especially have been gorging on squid, and when you clean them, that's all you see. This early squid concentration usually means the canyon's going to fish well through July.

The water conditions have been nearly perfect — light northwest winds all week, seas under 2 feet, and that beautiful blue water pushed right up against the shelf. Visibility's been 100 feet plus, and the current's been manageable at 1 to 1.5 knots on the wall.

One thing to watch: the temperature gradient is still pretty tight. You can go from 64-degree water to 68-degree water in less than a mile, especially along the northeast wall. That's where the fish are stacking, but it also means you need to pay attention to your electronics. The fish aren't spread out — they're concentrated in specific temperature pockets.

Looking ahead, this weekend's new moon is going to stir things up. The increased tidal flow should push more bait up from the deep water and spread the fish out along more of the wall structure. I'm expecting the bite to get even better, especially if this weather pattern holds.

The Washington always fishes early, and this year's no different. While everyone else is still waiting for their canyons to turn on, we're already into fish. That's the beauty of this piece of water — it sits in just the right spot to catch that first push of warm water, and the fish know it. If you're thinking about making the run, now's the time. The season's here.
